fact: Blood Falls runs clear when it emerges from beneath hundreds of metres of Antarctic ice. It turns blood-red only after its iron-rich, hypersaline brine hits air, oxidises and forms amorphous iron nanospheres.
locationContext: Taylor Valley · McMurdo Dry Valleys, East Antarctica

fact: Socotra is so biologically isolated that about 95% of its land-snail species and 90% of its reptile species occur nowhere else on Earth.
Rocks weighing as much as 320 kilograms can travel across Death Valley’s Racetrack Playa. Thin floating ice, shallow water and winds of only about 10 mph can move them in near-perfect synchrony.
Lençóis Maranhenses looks like a vast desert, yet rainwater alone creates thousands of clear seasonal lagoons between its white dunes, while some dunes migrate up to 25 metres in a year.
The 40-kilometre-wide Eye of the Sahara looks so much like an impact crater that scientists once classified it as one. It is actually the eroded remains of a colossal uplifted geologic dome.
locationContext: Adrar Plateau · central Mauritania, north-west Africa

fact: Mono Lake is roughly twice as salty as the ocean, and one of its islands contains lake-bottom mud that magma physically pushed above the water only a few centuries ago.
Lake Turkana is the world’s largest permanent desert lake, and fossils from its shores have contributed more to our understanding of human ancestry than those from any other place on Earth.
One lake holds about 20% of all the unfrozen freshwater on Earth. Lake Baikal is also the planet’s deepest lake and is estimated to be 25 million years old.

Lake Natron is too caustic for most familiar life, but its salt-loving microorganisms turn it red. Receding water also leaves moat-like channels that protect vast flamingo nesting grounds from predators.
locationContext: Arusha Region · northern Tanzania, East Africa

fact: When a thin layer of rainwater covers Salar de Uyuni, the world’s largest salt flat becomes a mirror spanning thousands of square kilometres, erasing the visual boundary between ground and sky.

Tsingy de Bemaraha is a forest made of razor-edged limestone needles. Its canyons and pinnacles isolate pockets of woodland so effectively that rare species evolved in tiny natural islands within the stone maze.

On Jeju Island, women divers, some in their 80s, descend about 10 metres without oxygen tanks and can work for up to seven hours a day. They hold their breath for every dive and make a unique sound when they surface.
locationContext: Jeju Province · South Korea, East Asia

source: ThisisFINLAND · Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
fact: Finland has been counted at 53.2 heavy-metal bands per 100,000 people, more per person than any other country. Tiny Lemi once entered 13 bands among only 3,076 residents and was crowned World Capital of Metal.

place: The world's most linguistically diverse country
fact: Papua New Guinea holds the record for the most living languages in one country: 840 were documented in 2019. Most of those languages are spoken by fewer than 1,000 people.
locationContext: Papua New Guinea · south-west Pacific, Oceania

fact: In the Voladores ceremony, four men launch themselves from a pole up to 40 metres high and spiral towards the ground on ropes. A fifth remains balanced on top, playing a flute and drum to honour the sun, winds and cardinal directions.
In Vanuatu, one finger turns sand, volcanic ash or clay into an intricate form of writing. The geometric drawings carry messages, stories and knowledge among roughly 80 ethnolinguistic groups.

The Baltic song and dance celebrations can assemble as many as 40,000 singers and dancers at once. Most are amateurs who rehearse for years before the enormous festivals held every four or five years.
locationContext: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania · Baltic region, Northern Europe

fact: Aka communities developed complex four-part contrapuntal singing without written notation. Singers improvise and alter their voices during a piece, making the music seem to change continuously, while children learn by joining rituals from an early age.
locationContext: South-western Central African Republic · Central Africa

country: Saudi Arabia, Oman and United Arab Emirates
fact: Camel herders use a sung oral tradition called Alheda'a to direct their animals. Camels are trained to distinguish calls for right and left, open their mouths on request, kneel to be ridden and assemble quickly during danger.
locationContext: Arabian Peninsula · Saudi Arabia, Oman and United Arab Emirates

fact: Falconry is practised by people of all ages in more than eighty countries. Skills are passed on through mentoring, within families and through clubs and schools, keeping a longstanding human partnership with birds alive.
On La Gomera, islanders can reproduce spoken Castilian Spanish as whistles, turning ordinary language into signals that carry across the island’s deep ravines.

In Catalonia, teams called colles build human towers several levels high in public squares. Hundreds of people can form the base, while a child climbs to the top and raises a hand to complete the castell.

photoCredit: U.S. National Park Service · public domain
fact: Garifuna songs and dances carry history and traditional knowledge across generations. Their living tradition blends African and Indigenous Caribbean influences and is shared by communities across four Central American countries.
locationContext: Caribbean coast · Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua

fact: An angklung is made from tuned bamboo tubes that sound when shaken. Because one instrument usually contributes only a note or chord, a complete melody depends on a whole group listening and playing together.
Kutiyattam is one of India's oldest living theatrical traditions. Performers use an intricate language of eye movements, facial expressions and hand gestures to unfold Sanskrit drama for an audience.
The enormous Epic of King Gesar survives not just as text but through singers and storytellers who perform its episodes. The tradition also feeds Tibetan opera, painting and other community arts.
locationContext: Tibetan Plateau and Inner Mongolia · China

place: Wine Horses of Caravaca de la Cruz
fact: Each May in Caravaca de la Cruz, horses wear spectacular cloaks embroidered with silk and gold thread. Four handlers then run beside each horse in a race up the steep approach to the castle.
locationContext: Caravaca de la Cruz, Murcia · south-eastern Spain

country: Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates
fact: Serving Arabic coffee is a carefully learned language of hospitality. The host prepares it for guests, serves the eldest or most important person first and pours small amounts so cups can be offered repeatedly.
locationContext: Arabian Peninsula · Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates

fact: Tibetan opera combines folk song, dance, storytelling, chanting and brightly painted masks in one performance tradition. Stories pass between generations while also teaching history and social values.

Deepavali brings families and communities together to light lamps, exchange gifts and sweets, share meals and celebrate with music, dance and rituals. The practices vary widely while the light remains a shared symbol of hope and renewal.
locationContext: India · South Asia and communities worldwide

fact: On Peru's Taquile Island, textile making is shared across the community: men traditionally knit while women spin wool and weave. Clothing is both practical and a visible record of social life and identity.
locationContext: Taquile Island, Lake Titicaca · southern Peru

fact: On Kihnu and Manija, women became the principal custodians of an island culture of runic songs, games, dances, wedding ceremonies and handicrafts while many men worked at sea.
locationContext: Kihnu and Manija islands · Gulf of Riga, Estonia

place: Bistritsa Babi of the Shoplouk region
fact: In Bistritsa, elderly women preserve an archaic form of Shoplouk polyphony alongside ring dances and seasonal rituals, passing the repertoire between generations.

place: Ritual dance of the royal drum
fact: Burundi's royal-drum tradition is not drumming alone: synchronized rhythms unfold with dancers, heroic poetry and traditional songs, turning the drum into a complete community performance.

place: Saman dance of the Gayo people
fact: Saman dancers perform in tight seated rows, creating rapid shared rhythms by clapping, striking their chests and thighs, tapping the ground and clicking their fingers while singing verses.
locationContext: Gayo communities · Aceh province, Sumatra, Indonesia

fact: Bauls are mystic minstrels who travel from village to village, singing a spiritual philosophy with simple instruments including the one-string ektara. Their song language keeps evolving to stay meaningful to new listeners.
locationContext: Rural Bangladesh · Bengal region, South Asia

fact: The Makishi masquerade appears at the end of mukanda, an annual initiation for boys aged roughly eight to twelve. Masked characters return to the community to celebrate and teach through dance and performance.
locationContext: North-western and western Zambia · southern Africa

fact: Across Mongolia each July, Naadam brings communities together for three traditional games: long-distance horse racing, wrestling and archery. Music, clothing, crafts and ritual surround the competitions.
At Oostduinkerke, fishers ride strong Brabant horses breast-deep into the North Sea. Each horse pulls a funnel-shaped net that sieves shrimp from the sand as the pair walks parallel to shore.
An official count on 28 August 2026 recorded just 222 Tristan da Cunha islanders. The entire resident community is centred on one settlement, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas.
locationContext: Edinburgh of the Seven Seas · Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic

fact: Sultan Kösen was first confirmed as the world's tallest living man in 2009 at 246.5 centimetres. Guinness also measured his hands at 28.5 centimetres from wrist to middle fingertip.
Jyoti Amge was measured at 62.8 centimetres tall in Nagpur on her eighteenth birthday, 16 December 2011, earning the Guinness title of shortest woman living.
The fujara is a Slovak shepherds' flute that can stand up to two metres long yet has only three finger holes. Players shape its deep, meditative music through breath and harmonic overtones.
Japanese washi is made by hand from paper-mulberry fibres through skills shared across whole communities. The craft produces remarkably strong paper despite its light, translucent appearance.

At Kyoto's Gion Matsuri, a local boy serves as a sacred messenger whose feet do not touch the ground from 13 July until the first parade ends. The largest hoko floats can reach 25 metres and weigh 12 tonnes.
The Royal Ballet of Cambodia uses codified hand gestures, controlled movement and elaborate costumes to enact legends. Its dancers were closely associated with the Khmer royal court for centuries.
Cremona's master luthiers hand-carve each violin from spruce and maple without prefabricated components, assembling over seventy distinct pieces in a tradition dating to 1539.
Capoeira players take turns sparring with flowing acrobatic kicks inside a singing circle, matching their tempo directly to the commanding rhythm of the berimbau bow.

photoCredit: InSapphoWeTrust from Los Angeles, Califo · CC BY-SA 2.0
fact: Mariachi ensembles bring together violins, trumpets, and the round-backed guitarrón bass to perform regional songs rooted in western Mexican rural gatherings.
Flamenco fuses passionate cante vocals, percussive guitar and dynamic footwork, expressing grief, longing, and joy across Andalusia's communities.
Born in the working-class ports of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, tango combines intimate partner dancing with the soulful, melancholic sound of the bandoneón accordion.
Gagaku has been performed in Japan's imperial court for more than a millennium, blending wind instruments like the sho mouth organ with ancient dance and precise ritual.
Al-Ayyala performers form two facing rows of men holding slender bamboo wands, moving together in rhythm with booming drums and chanted poetry celebrating bravery.
locationContext: Abu Dhabi and Al Ain · United Arab Emirates

photoCredit: Rollan Budi from Kuta, Bali,, Indonesia · CC BY-SA 2.0
fact: Kecak features a seated circle of up to one hundred men chanting continuous 'cak-cak' vocal rhythms, depicting epic Ramayana battles without any instrumental accompaniment.
A single master puppeteer, the dalang, manipulates intricate water-buffalo leather puppets behind a backlit screen for hours while singing and directing a full gamelan orchestra.
Noh drama uses carved wooden masks, stylised gliding footsteps, and poetic chanting to evoke supernatural tales on a minimalist cypress-wood stage.
The two-stringed wooden dombra is played solo to perform kuys—narrative musical poems that evoke historical legends, philosophical reflections, and steppe galloping.

place: Craftsmanship and performance art of the Tar
fact: The tar is an eleven-stringed, figure-of-eight lute carved from mulberry wood and covered in cattle heart-membrane, serving as the central lead instrument of Azerbaijani mugham.
locationContext: Baku and Shusha · Azerbaijan, South Caucasus

photoCredit: 단원 김홍도 (檀園 金弘道, 1745 - 1816 이후) · Public domain
fact: In Korean ssireum wrestling, two competitors grab a fabric belt called a satba tied around their opponent's waist and thigh, using technique and balance to topple the other without striking.

photoCredit: Pedro Ribeiro Simões from Lisboa, Portug · CC BY 2.0
fact: Fado blends poetic verses of longing and fate with the delicate twelve-string Portuguese guitar, originating in nineteenth-century maritime taverns of Lisbon.

photoCredit: Kevon Rhiney and Romain Cruse · CC BY 4.0
fact: Originating in Kingston in the late 1960s, reggae emerged as a voice for social justice, human rights, and spirituality, distinguished by its offbeat accents and heavy basslines.
Venice's Regata Storica has taken place along the Grand Canal since the thirteenth century, with costumed rowers propelling historic galleys standing up facing forward.
locationContext: Grand Canal, Venice · Veneto, north-eastern Italy

fact: Bertsolaris compose and sing rhymed, metred verses entirely on the spot in the ancient Basque language, debating philosophical and everyday prompts before thousands of spectators.
locationContext: Gipuzkoa and Biscay · Basque Country, northern Spain

fact: Frevo dancers in Recife sprint and jump through crowd-filled streets at breakneck speeds, executing acrobatic steps while balancing small, colourful open umbrellas.
locationContext: Recife and Olinda, Pernambuco · north-eastern Brazil

fact: Georgian polyphony is an ancient secular and sacred singing tradition featuring complex three-part vocal harmonies and unique scales that predated Western European notation.
With over three million saunas for 5.5 million inhabitants, the Finnish sauna is an essential communal ritual of cleansing, tranquility, and bonding practiced across all generations.
locationContext: Helsinki and Tampere · Finland, Northern Europe
